items.title: John Levy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Later on, Sparky Tavares and John Collins, whom I had knew and worked with years, were friends.

ctx.x: There was something special about your relationship with Joe Williams.

Yes it was. It was like brothers. It was a personal relationship. We loved each other like brothers. He would call me, no matter where he was, every day at 5 o’clock. That’s martini time. That’s when we have a drink. Out of all the males – people – men in my life, Joe Williams was the closest person, I think, in my life, as a male – men friends. I didn’t have many friends. I had a lot of acquaintances and people that I dealt with. Cannonball and Joe Williams were the two people – the two main people that were my…

items.title: 67250_John Collins oral history interview
items.q: that's where I met John Levy.

ctx.x: And she also -- while we were in Chicago she also worked for the Oriental Theatre. She used to do like a rehearsal pianist. At this time they wouldn't have a colored pianist in a band or anything, in a white band, but she did all the rehearsal work for the Oriental Theatre and the Chicago Theatre. She was a fine musician.

So I stayed there and struggled and thought, and it's -- you mentioned John Levy. I've got to tell you about John Levy. I -- my father was a postman, and he insisted that I go into the post office as a special delivery boy. I think I was around 16 years old then. But I wanted to play music, I didn't want to be in -- and I finally went down, just to appease my father, and that's where I met John Levy. This was in Chicago. John Levy was playing piano like Earl Hines, and he was a piano player. I think I was playing…
Did you start on guitar or did you start on banjo?
